cemc-fermat-2003-03.title: Straight line
cemc-fermat-2003-03.body:
Below the horizontal line the angles are $50^\circ+130^\circ=180^\circ$, so the horizontal line is straight. Above it, the angles $4x^\circ$, $x^\circ$ and the right angle together make $180^\circ$: $5x+90=180$, so $x=18$.

**Answer: (E) 18**

cemc-fermat-2003-04.title: Simulate
cemc-fermat-2003-04.body:
First time around she crosses out 1, 4, 7, 10. Remaining: 2, 3, 5, 6, 8, 9.

Counting every third remaining number after 10: 2, 3, **5**; then 6, 8, **9**; then 2, 3, **6**; then 8, 2, **3**. Left: 2 and 8, with sum $10$.

**Answer: (B) 10**

cemc-fermat-2003-05.title: Percent remaining
cemc-fermat-2003-05.body:
After losing $20\%$, the bear has $80\%$ of its mass: $0.8m=220$, so $m=275$ kg.

**Answer: (D) 275**

cemc-fermat-2003-05.title: Quarters
cemc-fermat-2003-05.body:
220 kg is $80\%$, so $20\%$ is a quarter of that, 55 kg. The original mass was $220+55=275$ kg.

**Answer: (D) 275**

cemc-fermat-2003-07.title: Rise in level
cemc-fermat-2003-07.body:
Half full means the water is 15 cm deep. The base area is $20\times40=800\text{ cm}^2$, so $4000\text{ cm}^3$ raises the level by $4000\div800=5$ cm. New depth: $20$ cm.

**Answer: (C) 20 cm**

cemc-fermat-2003-07.title: Total volume
cemc-fermat-2003-07.body:
Initially the water volume is $800\times15=12\,000\text{ cm}^3$. After adding, $16\,000\text{ cm}^3$, so the depth is $16\,000\div800=20$ cm.

**Answer: (C) 20 cm**

cemc-fermat-2003-08.title: Perpendicular slopes
cemc-fermat-2003-08.body:
The slope of $BC$ is $\dfrac{7-(-4)}{6-9}=-\dfrac{11}{3}$. Perpendicular slopes multiply to $-1$, so the slope of $AD$ is $\dfrac{3}{11}$. (The coordinates of $A$ are not needed.)

**Answer: (A) $\frac{3}{11}$**

cemc-fermat-2003-11.title: List the routes
cemc-fermat-2003-11.body:
From the diagram: 2 edges from $A$ to $X$, 1 from $A$ to $Y$, 1 from $X$ to $Y$, 1 from $X$ to $B$, and 3 from $Y$ to $B$.

- $A\to X\to B$: $2\times1=2$ routes
- $A\to X\to Y\to B$: $2\times1\times3=6$ routes
- $A\to Y\to B$: $1\times3=3$ routes

There are 11 routes, 8 of which pass through $X$. The probability is $\frac{8}{11}$.

**Answer: (A) $\frac{8}{11}$**

cemc-fermat-2003-11.title: Count paths into each point
cemc-fermat-2003-11.body:
Number of ways to reach each point: $X$: 2. $Y$: from $A$ (1) plus from $X$ ($2$) $=3$. $B$: from $X$ (2) plus three edges from $Y$ ($3\cdot3=9$) $=11$. Routes avoiding $X$: $1\cdot3=3$. So $11-3=8$ pass through $X$, probability $\frac8{11}$.

**Answer: (A) $\frac{8}{11}$**

cemc-fermat-2003-12.title: Pythagoras
cemc-fermat-2003-12.body:
$AC=\sqrt{10^2+10^2}=10\sqrt2\approx14.14$. Since $D$ is on $AC$ with $CD=10$, $AD=AC-CD\approx4.14$, closest to $4$.

**Answer: (E) 4**

cemc-fermat-2003-13.title: Solve for x and y
cemc-fermat-2003-13.body:
Adding the equations: $2x=4$, $x=2$, so $y=-1$. Then $x^2-y^2=4-1=3$ and $2^3=8$.

**Answer: (B) 8**

cemc-fermat-2003-14.title: Exterior angles at P
cemc-fermat-2003-14.body:
Since $\angle PRM=125^\circ$, its supplements are $\angle QRP=\angle NRM=55^\circ$.

In triangle $QPR$ (angles $a^\circ$ at $Q$ and $55^\circ$ at $R$), the exterior angle at $P$ is $\angle APR=a+55$.

In triangle $APN$ (angles $55^\circ$ at $A$ and $b^\circ$ at $N$), the exterior angle at $P$ is $\angle QPN=55+b$.

These two angles at $P$ lie on the straight line $AQ$, so $(a+55)+(55+b)=180$ and $a+b=70$.

**Answer: (A) 70**

cemc-fermat-2003-14.title: Triangles through M
cemc-fermat-2003-14.body:
In triangle $RMN$: $\angle NRM=55^\circ$, so $\angle RMN=180-55-b=125-b$, and so $\angle AMQ=180-(125-b)=55+b$.

In triangle $AQM$: $55+a+(55+b)=180$, so $a+b=70$.

**Answer: (A) 70**

cemc-fermat-2003-15.title: Divisibility
cemc-fermat-2003-15.body:
If the triangle has side $T$ and the square side $S$, then $3T=4S$. So $4\mid3T$, and since $\gcd(3,4)=1$, $4\mid T$. The only choice divisible by 4 is $20$ (then $S=15$).

**Answer: (D) 20**

cemc-fermat-2003-15.title: Test the choices
cemc-fermat-2003-15.body:
The perimeter $3T$ must be divisible by 4: $3,30,54,60,75$ — only $60$ is, from $T=20$.

**Answer: (D) 20**

cemc-fermat-2003-17.title: Isosceles triangle, then 30-60-90
cemc-fermat-2003-17.body:
Let $\angle ABC=\theta$, so $\angle ADC=2\theta$. The exterior angle of triangle $ABD$ at $D$ is $2\theta=\theta+\angle BAD$, so $\angle BAD=\theta$ and triangle $ABD$ is isosceles with $DA=DB=2x$.

In right triangle $ADC$, the hypotenuse $AD=2x$ is twice $DC=x$, so it is a 30-60-90 triangle with $\angle ADC=60^\circ$. Then $\theta=30^\circ$, and in triangle $ABC$ (30-60-90 with $BC=3x$ opposite the $60^\circ$ angle), $AB=\frac{2}{\sqrt3}\cdot3x=2\sqrt3\,x$.

**Answer: (C) $2\sqrt3\,x$**

cemc-fermat-2003-19.title: Two right triangles
cemc-fermat-2003-19.body:
Put the wall foot at $W$ and the point under $S$ at $F$. Then $B$ is 1 m up, $T$ is 3 m up, and $S$ is 4 m up and 3 m out.

From $S$, the point $B$ is 3 m across and 3 m down, so line $SB$ makes $45^\circ$ with the vertical $SF$. The point $T$ is 3 m across and 1 m down, so $\tan\angle TSF=\frac31$, giving $\angle TSF\approx71.6^\circ$.

$\angle TSB=71.6^\circ-45^\circ\approx26.6^\circ$, closest to $27^\circ$.

**Answer: (A) $27^\circ$**

cemc-fermat-2003-19.title: Difference of angles formula
cemc-fermat-2003-19.body:
Measured from the horizontal through $S$, $SB$ is $45^\circ$ below ($\tan=\frac33$) and $ST$ is at angle $\alpha$ below with $\tan\alpha=\frac13$. Then $\tan\angle TSB=\tan(45^\circ-\alpha)=\dfrac{1-\frac13}{1+\frac13}=\frac12$, so $\angle TSB=\arctan\frac12\approx26.6^\circ\approx27^\circ$.

**Answer: (A) $27^\circ$**

cemc-fermat-2003-20.title: Discriminant
cemc-fermat-2003-20.body:
$\frac cb=\frac ba$ gives $b^2=ac$. The discriminant is $b^2-4ac=ac-4ac=-3ac<0$, so the parabola never meets the $x$-axis. Since $a>0$ it opens upward, so it lies entirely above the $x$-axis.

**Answer: (C) entirely above the $x$-axis**

cemc-fermat-2003-20.title: An example
cemc-fermat-2003-20.body:
Take $a=b=c=1$ (ratio 1): $y=x^2+x+1=\left(x+\frac12\right)^2+\frac34>0$ for all $x$. The graph is entirely above the $x$-axis, which rules out every other choice; the discriminant argument shows this always happens.

**Answer: (C) entirely above the $x$-axis**

cemc-fermat-2003-21.title: Find the cycle
cemc-fermat-2003-21.body:
The terms are $6,3,10,5,16,8,4,2,1,4,2,1,\ldots$ From the 7th term on, the sequence repeats $4,2,1$. The 9th term is 1, and since the cycle has length 3, every term whose position is a multiple of 3 (from the 9th on) is 1. So $t_{99}=1$ and $t_{100}=4$.

**Answer: (D) 4**

cemc-fermat-2003-22.title: Parallel diagonals
cemc-fermat-2003-22.body:
Triangles $BCD$ and $CDE$ share base $CD$ and have equal area, so $B$ and $E$ are equally far from line $CD$: $BE\parallel CD$. Likewise every diagonal is parallel to the opposite side.

Let $X$ be the intersection of $BD$ and $CE$. Since $BD\parallel AE$ and $CE\parallel AB$, $ABXE$ is a parallelogram, so $[BXE]=[EAB]=1$.

Let $[CXD]=t$. Then $[CXB]=[BCD]-t=1-t$ and $[EXD]=[CDE]-t=1-t$. Triangles $CXD$ and $CXB$ have the same height from $C$, so $\frac{DX}{XB}=\frac{t}{1-t}$. Since $CD\parallel BE$, triangles $CXD$ and $EXB$ are similar with ratio $\frac{DX}{XB}$, so $\frac{t}{1}=\left(\frac{t}{1-t}\right)^2$, i.e. $(1-t)^2=t$, $t^2-3t+1=0$, and $t=\frac{3-\sqrt5}{2}$ (it must be less than 1).

Area of pentagon $=[EAB]+[BXE]+[CXB]+[EXD]+[CXD]=1+1+(1-t)+(1-t)+t=4-t=\frac{5+\sqrt5}{2}\approx3.618$, closest to $3.62$.

**Answer: (A) 3.62**

cemc-fermat-2003-22.title: Assume a regular pentagon
cemc-fermat-2003-22.body:
The answer does not depend on the shape, so take a regular pentagon. Then the pentagon is $[ABC]+[ACE]+[CDE]=2+[ACE]$.

In a regular pentagon with side $s$, the diagonal is $d=\varphi s$ with $\varphi=\frac{1+\sqrt5}2=2\cos36^\circ$. Triangle $ABC$ has sides $s,s$ with included angle $108^\circ$; triangle $ACE$ has sides $d,d$ with included angle $36^\circ$. So

$$\frac{[ACE]}{[ABC]}=\frac{\frac12d^2\sin36^\circ}{\frac12s^2\sin108^\circ}=\frac{\varphi^2\sin36^\circ}{\sin72^\circ}=\frac{\varphi^2\sin36^\circ}{2\sin36^\circ\cos36^\circ}=\frac{\varphi^2}{\varphi}=\varphi.$$

With $[ABC]=1$, $[ACE]=\varphi\approx1.618$, and the pentagon has area $2+\varphi=\frac{5+\sqrt5}{2}\approx3.618$, closest to $3.62$.

**Answer: (A) 3.62**

cemc-fermat-2003-23.title: Half-edges
cemc-fermat-2003-23.body:
Let the edges be $2a$, $2b$, $2c$, with the corner at the origin. The face centres are $(a,b,0)$, $(a,0,c)$, $(0,b,c)$. Their distances squared are $a^2+b^2$, $b^2+c^2$, $a^2+c^2$ (e.g. $(a,b,0)$ to $(a,0,c)$ gives $b^2+c^2$).

So $a^2+b^2=16$, $b^2+c^2=25$, $a^2+c^2=36$ (in some order — the volume is symmetric). Adding: $a^2+b^2+c^2=\frac{77}{2}$, so $c^2=\frac{45}{2}$, $a^2=\frac{27}{2}$, $b^2=\frac52$.

$a^2b^2c^2=\frac{27\cdot5\cdot45}{8}=\frac{6075}{8}$, so $abc=\frac{45\sqrt3}{2\sqrt2}$. The volume is $8abc=\frac{180\sqrt3}{\sqrt2}=90\sqrt6$.

**Answer: (C) $90\sqrt6$**

cemc-fermat-2003-24.title: Base 3
cemc-fermat-2003-24.body:
The expression is $\prod_{k=0}^{6}\left(1+2^kx^{3^k}\right)^2=\prod_{k=0}^{6}\left(1+2^{k+1}x^{3^k}+2^{2k}x^{2\cdot3^k}\right)$.

Each term of the product picks, for each $k$, the exponent $d_k3^k$ with $d_k\in\{0,1,2\}$ and coefficient $1$, $2^{k+1}$ or $2^{2k}$ respectively. We need $\sum d_k3^k=2003$, which is a base-3 representation, so it is unique: $2003=2202012_3$, i.e. $d_6=2,d_5=2,d_4=0,d_3=2,d_2=0,d_1=1,d_0=2$.

The coefficient is the product of the chosen coefficients: $k=0$: $2^0$; $k=1$: $2^{2}$; $k=3$: $2^6$; $k=5$: $2^{10}$; $k=6$: $2^{12}$ (and $1$ for $k=2,4$). Total: $2^{0+2+6+10+12}=2^{30}$.

**Answer: (C) $2^{30}$**

cemc-fermat-2003-25.title: Factor a difference of squares
cemc-fermat-2003-25.body:
We need $4+2112=2116=46^2$ (true), $n+2112=x^2$ and $4n+2112=y^2$ with positive integers $x,y$; since $n>0$, $x>46$.

Then $4x^2-y^2=4\cdot2112-2112=3\cdot2112=6336$, so $(2x-y)(2x+y)=6336=2^6\cdot3^2\cdot11$.

Let $2x+y=A$, $2x-y=B$. Their product is even and their sum $4x$ is even, so both are even. If both were $\equiv2\pmod4$, their product would contain only $2^2$, not $2^6$; and if just one were, $A+B=4x$ would fail. So both are multiples of 4. Write $A=4p$, $B=4q$: $pq=396=2^2\cdot3^2\cdot11$, $x=p+q$, $y=2(p-q)$, with $p>q$.

$396$ has $3\cdot3\cdot2=18$ divisors, giving 9 pairs $(p,q)$: $(396,1),(198,2),(132,3),(99,4),(66,6),(44,9),(36,11),(33,12),(22,18)$, with $x=p+q=397,200,135,103,72,53,47,45,40$. We need $x>46$: the first 7 pairs. Then $n=x^2-2112$ gives $155497, 37888, 16113, 8497, 3072, 697, 97$ (each also gives $4n+2112=y^2$ by construction).

There are $7$ values.

**Answer: (B) 7**
